That substitution is the table's one inference and route 6 tests it: the label file makes itmcqf3 the facet's only reverse-worded item, and in the live data it is the only item with a negative mean correlation against the rest, -0.420 (pairwise -0.385, -0.457, -0.417) against +0.253, +0.240 and +0.257 for the other three, which intercorrelate +0.566 to +0.611. What this does NOT do is separate itmcqf1, itmcqf2 and itmcqf4 from one another; no per-item statistics are available to do that, the article being paywalled, hence PARTIAL. validate_items.R reports item and resp sets matching live data (4 items, 2,028 rows).

The three questions are reproduced verbatim in the S1 File's 'Part 4 : Additional questions' block, and verify_shu_2025_translation_add.R re-checks each shipped item_text against that cached file rather than re-checking counts. Two codes are pinned by content match. The third, addcompetitioninreha, rests on elimination alone: its code reads 'competition' where the remaining question concerns study pressure and career plans. No data-side route exists to separate the three -- the article publishes no per-item statistics and the items share no structure a statistic could distinguish -- and the one asymmetry that might have helped, addcompetitioninreha using resp 1-4 against 1-5 for the other two, cannot be used because the S1 File states no response options for any of them. Hence PARTIAL on 2 of 3 items pinned.

Nothing to check: the Oxford ARC data paper's own processed_data_dictionary.csv keys every one of the 44 live item codes to its Field_Label verbatim, and the codes are self-describing besides (activity_exercise_outside, media_why_tv_news), so no order or position was inferred at any point. validate_items.R reports item and resp sets matching live data (44 items, 179,937 rows). audit_batch.R's WARN on this table is the instrument's conditional structure, not a defect: the 36 reason items fall into six clusters of six with near-identical n inside each cluster (2,264-2,304, 2,410-2,465, 2,883-2,955, 4,201-4,242, 4,301-4,545, 6,193-6,277), because each medium's six reasons were asked only of respondents who used that medium, and the 8 hours-per-day items run 4,699-6,480. The same WARN's blank-option_text half is the two response formats: hours per day is a quantity and carries no option label by design.

Three routes. (1) The published DERS-36 numbering is the 41-item pool minus items 2, 11, 13, 18, 36, renumbered ascending; under that rule Table III's 11 reverse-scored items land on exactly positions 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 10, 17, 20, 22, 24, 34. (2) Those same 11 positions are pinned independently by the deposit: dropping DERS_37_POST and reversing them reproduces DERS_SUM_POST for 90 of 90 complete rows, against a best-of-36 alternative drop of 42 of 90 and 6 of 90 for no reverses -- which also shows the items are stored raw and that column 37 is unscored. (3) Grouping the 36 columns by Table III's six factors gives mean within-subscale r = 0.503, above the maximum (0.440) of 2000 same-sized random groupings, p = 0.0005, so each item is pinned to its subscale. LIMIT, and the reason this is PARTIAL not VERIFIED: routes 1-2 fix polarity class and the unscored column, route 3 fixes subscale membership, but two items sharing a subscale and a polarity are still interchangeable on the evidence. Their individual assignment rests on the monotone renumbering rather than on the data. A rival ordering that preserved both polarity and subscale would not be detected.
